name: Victor Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Victor, 27, and I work in trade marketing at Kettleby Coffee, a roaster whose bags and pods are sold in supermarkets. I live with my girlfriend Ilona, who's a dental hygienist, in a rented flat near the ring road. I've been at Kettleby about fourteen months; before that I did a graduate scheme at a drinks distributor that didn't keep me on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My job is the stuff that makes people pick our coffee off the shelf: the promotions calendar, the shelf signs, the leaflets, and the copy for supermarket websites. Twice a month I go out to stores and run a tasting stand, which I actually love, because you see people's faces. I use an AI tool sometimes for promo wording, but my boss Marta says I need to get sharper at the numbers. What wears me out is the promo forecasts, guessing how many bags we'll sell at two for five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, every new thing gets oversold. At work I'd say let's use the bits that help, like quick promo wording, and move on. Online I'd probably share a funny chart about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay. Coffee doesn't go out of fashion, Kettleby's growing, and half my value is being in the stores. My real worry is just getting better at the forecasts so Marta stops sighing at my spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and ask Marta to sit with me on forecasts once a month. I'd keep using the AI tool for promo wording, maybe a bit more. And I'd keep putting 200 a month away, we're at about four months now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. A bit flat maybe, because the big talk turned out to be small. Mostly I'd be glad to get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half your value is being in the stores. Tell me about a tasting day.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I was in a big supermarket on a Saturday, handing out little cups of our dark roast. An old man came back three times to my tasting stand and then bought four bags of coffee. You don't get that from a spreadsheet. He told me his wife only drinks ours now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ilona plan, if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep saving for a deposit, maybe buy in two or three years. Ilona wants a dog first, I want a flat first. That's our biggest argument, which says a lot about how calm things are.

say: I'd say every new thing gets **oversold**.
I'd use the bits that help, like **promo wording**, and move on.
think: Coffee's **growing**, and half his value is being **in stores**.
His real worry is getting better at **forecasts**.
do: Ask Marta to coach him on **forecasts** monthly.
Keep saving **200 a month** on top of four months saved.
feel: **Fine**, a bit flat that the big talk turned small.
S0.quote: An old man came back three times to my tasting stand and then bought four bags of coffee. You don't get that from a spreadsheet.
fieldNote: His **in-store tasting days** are his anchor and joy.
He feels **secure** because the brand is growing.
The household's biggest argument is **dog or flat**, a sign of calm.

steps.text: Ask Marta for a monthly session on promo forecasts
Keep saving 200 a month toward a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift and people should learn the tools, without panicking. At work I'd volunteer to test whatever new forecasting software we get. I'd keep it practical online, no doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the office half of my job shrinks fast. Shelf copy, website listings and promo forecasts are exactly what the software does, and Marta could probably cover them with a tool. The tasting days stay, but nobody employs someone full-time just for two Saturdays a month of coffee tastings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marta if I could move toward field work, visiting stores and managing the tasting team, since that's the part a person still does. I'd take the supermarket's own course on their new promo tools, which is free for suppliers. And I'd push our savings from four to six months by pausing the deposit plan for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit anxious. I'd want to see the tools working before I bet everything on them. But I'd know my desk work is on borrowed time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pausing the deposit. How would Ilona take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not well. Ilona's job feels safe to her, teeth still need cleaning, so she'd say why should we wait. I'd say because if I lose half my income, the bank won't care about her teeth argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kettleby would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, who does the supermarket listings full time. That's all screen work, and he's been there eight years. I'd worry he hasn't noticed what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from government and companies, now, not after. I'd tell people at work to save what they can. I'd probably sign petitions, but I'm not a marcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the desk half of my job goes in 2028, and the store half lasts until robots come around 2031. So maybe I keep some work for three extra years, but at half the pay. That's not enough to live on long-term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into field sales for Kettleby or another food brand, the people who visit supermarkets and set up displays. That's hands-on, so it lasts longer. I'd cut our spending hard, cancel the car lease if needed, and Ilona and I would hold off on the dog and the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'm the type who waits for proof, and here there's no time to wait. I'd feel like I was running before I'd checked which way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move into field sales. Do you have the skills for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. I can talk to store managers, I'm good on tasting days. But I'm not a natural seller, and I'd have to learn fast. Marta knows the head of field sales, so I'd ask her for an introduction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car lease, which is 280 a month. Ilona can bike to work, and I'd borrow her dad's car for store visits if I had to. Then holidays.

I'd tell colleagues to **save** and sign petitions, not march.
think: The **desk half** goes in 2028; the store half lasts to **2031**.
Three extra years at **half pay** isn't enough long-term.

feel: **Alarmed**, with no time to wait for proof.

fieldNote: He maps the **robot delay** directly onto his split job.

Ilona's **trade job** and her dad's car are household fallbacks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we should be training people now. At work I'd push for Kettleby to run training on the new tools. I'd keep it calm online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have about three good years before the desk side really goes. That's enough time to get into field sales properly and get good at it. I'd want to watch what other brands do first, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools in year one so I'm useful while things change. By year two I'd apply for field sales roles, maybe at a bigger food company with more store visits. And we'd still save, aiming for six months, but buy a small flat if prices allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I believe in. Five years is quick, but I can see the steps. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said watch what other brands do. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big cereal and biscuit brands, because they always move first. If the big cereal and biscuit brands' field teams are growing in 2028, that's my signal to move. If they're shrinking, I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 32 in 2031. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd want my life sorted, flat and maybe a kid on the way. So I'd want a job that lasts to 2034 at least. Field sales does that, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan sensibly, so let's not panic. At work I'd talk about which roles grow. With friends I'd say it's like any big change, you adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for a good while. I'd move into field sales or account management, where you meet people. By 2036 I'd be 37 and probably in a store-facing role that lasts until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Kettleby for a few years, learn the tools, and get a promotion if I can. Around year three I'd move to field sales or managing a tasting team. We'd buy the flat in the next two years and get the dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. I'd still have the end point in my head. But ten years is long enough for me to be careful and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'careful and right'. Is there a risk you're too careful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably. I wait for proof, and sometimes the proof comes late. Ilona says I'll still be watching other brands in 2035. She might be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2039, when robots come for the store side too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd be 40 when robots come for the store side, and I'd need a third plan. Maybe by then there's a system to support people, but I can't count on that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm someone who waits for proof, and there's no time to wait. What would help is companies giving people a few months' notice and paying for training into roles like field sales.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that the bit of my job I love most, standing in a shop handing out coffee, is the bit that might last longest. That's a strange comfort.

headlineQuote: The bit of my job I love most, standing in a shop handing out coffee, is the bit that might last longest.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old trade marketer** at a coffee roaster, living with Ilona, a dental hygienist.
He splits his job into a **desk half** and a **store half** of tasting days.
He uses AI **now and then** and waits for proof before moving.
Faster scenarios push him toward **field sales**, using the robot delay.
He keeps family plans, like a **flat and a dog**, at the centre.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he waits for proof and there'd be no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice and paid training** into roles like field sales.
